title: GPT-6 Astra Can Build 3D Worlds to Learn Anything (title from repo catalog .prism/shared/pot/catalog_local.json; no description file present)
core_takeaway: The presenter used OpenAI Codex driving GPT-6 Astra, plus Blender for asset creation and Babylon.js for browser rendering, to autonomously build and host a 12-station 3D learning world that teaches how Codex itself works. The whole run took ~18 hours and ~8 million tokens on Astra medium, unattended, because the plan — not the prompting — carried the weight: an explicit definition of done, a small visual target package rendered before committing to full production, a failure-mode test matrix executed in the agent's internal browser, and a quality rubric for the 'vibe' dimensions a test suite cannot assert. The claim is that this pattern generalizes to any subject better learned spatially than from a PDF.
key_points: Blender is installed through Codex's plugin menu rather than manually: two plugins exist ('Game Development Studio' and 'build 3D game rooms'), and the plugin carries a skill that acts as a cheat sheet for building 3D experiences with less back-and-forth.
Babylon.js is the piece most people miss: Blender creates the 3D assets, Babylon renders them so the world is actually playable in a browser.

The plan opens with a definition-of-done sentence enumerating scope — 12 core missions, three chapters, one capstone, a feature atlas, downloadable resources — which also implies browser storage for the downloadable markdown/PDF.

Before full production the agent was told to produce a visual target package: arrival shot, mascot close-up, one learning exhibit, a material sheet, and a 15-20 second motion sample, to catch blurry labels, bad lighting and missing backdrops cheaply.
Testing was scoped to the agent's internal browser specifically so it would not contend with the user's own Chrome session during a multi-hour unattended run.

The test matrix names concrete failure modes: corrupted old saves, disabled storage, missing assets, slow networks (to measure render latency), aborted downloads, decoder failures, graphics context loss, and unsupported graphics.
A rubric covers what tests cannot: mascot identity, character performance, spatiality, lighting, teaching quality, camera navigation, and non-sequential station hopping without breaking fluidity.

Deliverables were demanded explicitly: source Blender masters, asset provenance per scene element (so a broken piece is swapped rather than the world rebuilt), a reproducible build, a lesson source catalog, browser visual evidence, and the final hosted URL.

The run cost ~18 hours and ~8M tokens on Astra medium, executed via a '/goal' loop because Astra was behaving lazily at the time; the presenter says he would now plan on Astra medium/high and execute with Soul or Luna instead of using /goal.
why_it_matters: This is a concrete recipe for long-horizon unattended agent work: the leverage is entirely in plan artifacts — definition of done, cheap visual pre-vis, explicit failure-mode matrix, provenance requirements, and a rubric for subjective quality — not in a clever prompt. For a creative technologist, the Blender-to-Babylon pipeline plus asset provenance is a directly reusable spine for generative 3D deliverables, and the internal-browser testing constraint is the small detail that makes overnight runs survivable.

oss.name: Blender
oss.note: Used to generate all 3D assets; installed and driven by the agent through a Codex plugin that bundles a 3D-building skill, with 'source Blender masters' demanded as a deliverable.

oss.name: Babylon.js
oss.note: The browser 3D engine that renders the Blender-produced assets so the learning world is playable on the web — the dependency the presenter says he did not anticipate needing.

oss.name: Mermaid
oss.note: Used in the plan to diagram the frame-by-frame player flow so the agent could reason about and test the sequence.

oss.name: OpenAI Codex
oss.note: The agent harness running GPT-6 Astra that planned, built, tested and shipped the world, including plugin install and internal-browser testing.
